title: Span and Memory, including C# 14 conversions
hook: Span is how you point at existing memory without a new string. Memory is how that pointer survives an await. C# 14 finally treats those conversions as first-class in the language.

sections.heading: ref struct versus a heap buffer ticket
sections.prose: `Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` are `ref struct` types. They can wrap an array, a stackalloc buffer, unmanaged memory, or a slice of another span. Because they may refer to the stack, the compiler forbids class fields, boxing, and capturing them into an async state machine. `Memory<T>` / `ReadOnlyMemory<T>` are structs that can live on the heap; they are a ticket to later produce a `Span` with `.Span`. Microsoft’s usage guidelines: synchronous APIs take `Span`/`ReadOnlySpan`; asynchronous APIs take `Memory`/`ReadOnlyMemory` and must not use that memory after the `Task` completes. If you own an `IMemoryOwner<T>`, you dispose or transfer ownership — not both. High-concurrency attempt-submit code that `Substring`s every payload field is paying GEN0 for data that already sat in a byte buffer.

snippets.label: Sync span, async memory
snippets.explanation: The async method stores Memory, not Span. After await it takes .Span only in a synchronous burst. That is the guideline, not a style preference.

sections.heading: C# 14 implicit span conversions
sections.prose: C# 14 introduces first-class support for `Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>` in the language: implicit conversions among `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `Span<T>`, and `T[]`, better extension-method receivers, composition with other conversions, and generic type inference that used to fail. Before that, you wrote `.AsSpan()` everywhere and watched overload resolution pick the `string` API that allocates. Collection expressions (C# 12) already let you write `ReadOnlySpan<char> c = ['a', 'b'];`. C# 13 allowed `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` and `allows ref struct` so generic helpers can accept spans. C# 14 is the conversion story that makes those APIs feel like arrays. Set `introducedIn` in your notes: this is a C# 14 / .NET 10 talking point, not “spans were added last year.”

snippets.label: Natural span parameters on .NET 10
snippets.explanation: On C# 14, array-to-span conversions are implicit in more overload and inference cases. You still use AsSpan on string because string is not T[].

sections.heading: C# 13: more places spans are legal
sections.prose: `ref` locals and `ref struct` locals may appear in `async` methods and iterators, but not across `await` or `yield return`. `ref struct` types may implement interfaces, yet converting a `ref struct` to the interface type would box and is forbidden. Generic type parameters can opt in with `allows ref struct`. Together these let library code take `Span<T>` where C# 12 forced `T[]` or `IEnumerable<T>`. Interviews that stop at “span cannot be in async” are stuck on C# 12 rules.

interviewTakeaways: Span is a ref struct for synchronous views; Memory is the async-safe ticket to a span.
C# 14 adds implicit conversions among Span, ReadOnlySpan, and arrays.
C# 13 widened where ref structs may appear; it did not make Span awaitable.
commonPitfalls: Holding a Span across await — the compiler should stop you; a Memory field you keep after the Task completes is a silent use-after-free of a rented buffer.
Calling ToString() on a span in a hot loop, which allocates the string you were trying to avoid.
Using Memory when the method is fully synchronous — you lost readonly-ness and invited storage bugs.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `subarray` views the same ArrayBuffer; `slice` copies. Span is the view; ToArray/ToString is the copy. JS has no ref-struct rule because the GC model differs.
